title: Sentencing hearing for cop in woman's custody death starts with twist
article: A hearing to determine if a London police officer should go to jail for his role in the death of an Oneida woman began with a twist Thursday: his lawyer wants the conviction thrown out.
"I certainly am fresh eyes," on the case, lawyer Alan Gold told the court, an understatement in the midst of two tangles of legal arguments at a sentencing hearing in London.
Fresh eyes aside, Superior Court Justice Renee Pomerance said she wasn't even sure she could throw out the conviction, it had been upheld by the Ontario Court of Appeal.
"It's not clear to me if I can overturn a finding of guilt by Court of Appeal," she said.
Pomerance reserved her decision on the motion to overturn the conviction and acquit Const. Nicholas Doering, and on the sentencing arguments that made up the second part of the hearing.

The Crown is seeking a jail sentence of six to nine months on Doering's conviction for failing to provide the necessaries of life to Debra Chrisjohn of the Oneida of the Thames First Nation, who died Sept. 6, 2016.
"This is a serious and grave offence" with a "devastating ripple effect on her family and friends," assistant Crown Samuel Greene told the court.
Doering's did not provide Chrisjohn with medical help that might have saved her life, Greene said.
The woman was "extremely vulnerable" while in Doering's custody and "completely dependent" on him for her safety, Greene said.
Doering's lawyer is seeking a conditional sentence of 12 months, if the conviction holds.

"There is no justification in policy and principle to put that man in jail," Gold said. "You certainly should not jail a person with PTSD and panic attacks unless it's absolutely necessary for some reason, especially when they're going to be in protective custody."
What his client has gone through, from media exposure to psychological problems, already provides "enormous deterrence for other police officers," Gold added.
Doering arrested Chrisjohn, 39, about 5:40 p.m. Sept. 6, 2016, in London after she was found walking into traffic while high on crystal methamphetamine.
He asked an EMS supervisor if Chrisjohn should be taken to hospital. That officer looked into the window of the police cruiser and said no, according to court testimony.
The OPP agreed to take custody of Chrisjohn and OPP officers met Doering at a Tim Horton's just before 7 p.m. for the transfer.
Doering transferred her to Elgin OPP custody on an outstanding arrest warrant, telling OPP officers Chrisjohn had been medically assessed.
Shortly after the OPP took Chrisjohn into custody, paramedics were called to the Elgin OPP detachment, where they found her motionless and breathing irregularly. Chrisjohn died in hospital.
A post-mortem determined the mother of 11 died from cardiac arrest connected to crystal meth use, court heard.

Doering, 31, became the first Canadian police officer convicted of criminal negligence causing death in 2019 after Pomerance found him guilty of that offence and of failing to provide the necessaries of life.
The Ontario Court of Appeal overturned the conviction for criminal negligence causing death.
The Court of Appeal took issue with Pomerance's conclusion that Doering deliberately misled OPP officers when he said Chrisjohn had been assessed by paramedics.
Doering reasonably believed the EMS officer had assessed Chrisjohn in some fashion and didn't need medical attention, the court concluded.
The Court of Appeal also concluded, however, that Pomerance was correct in ruling Doering had failed to provide the necessaries of life to Chrisjohn.

"The trial judge could conclude that a reasonably prudent police officer would have appreciated the need for medical advice and assistance at some point before transferring Ms. Chrisjohn to the OPP. That same reasonable, prudent police officer would also have been aware that Ms. Chrisjohn's life was endangered by the failure to seek medical advice and intervention," the Court of Appeal ruled.
But Doering's lawyer argued Thursday that the overturning of the one conviction and weaknesses in the Crown's case gave Justice Pomerance an opening to overturn the other conviction.
At trial and on appeal, the Crown never alleged any omission on Doering's part during the drive was "a causal factor in the death," Gold said.
The Crown's case focused on the allegation Doering had misled the OPP, Gold said.

Now that that more serious conviction based on that allegation, criminal negligence causing death, had been overturned, Pomerance could overturn the other conviction, or at least send it back to the appeal court, Gold said.
If there was a legal mistake, "I am probably not the person to correct it," Pomerance told him.
It wasn't a legal mistake as much as a mistake in how the case was presented, Gold said.
